title: Research Fan-Out — Four Lenses, Three Judges, One Call
description: An open question answered by deliberate disagreement: four researchers work independent lenses in parallel, cheap probes do the fetching, and three judges score the synthesis before a recommendation is allowed out.

nodes.name: Question
nodes.description: Should the ingest pipeline move off Kafka to Redpanda before the Q3 traffic step-up?
nodes.output:
Asked by: platform team
Deadline: decision needed before Q3 capacity planning closes
Constraint: ingest currently peaks at 240k msg/s; Q3 forecast is 600k msg/s
Existing: 3-broker Kafka on MSK, 14 consumer groups, 2 engineers who know it well

nodes.name: Decompose question
nodes.description: Splits the question into four lenses chosen to disagree with each other, so the answer is not just one model's first instinct restated four times.
nodes.prompt:
Decompose this migration question into independent research lenses.

The lenses must be capable of reaching different conclusions — pick angles that pull against each other rather than four flavours of the same analysis. For each lens, state what evidence would change its mind.
nodes.output:
Four lenses, deliberately opposed:

  ops    — what does day-two operation cost, who carries the pager
  perf   — does Kafka actually fail at 600k msg/s on this hardware, or do we assume it does
  cost   — total cost of ownership including the migration itself, not just steady state
  risk   — what breaks during cutover, and what is the blast radius

Falsifiers stated per lens so a null result is still a result.

nodes.name: Lens: operations
nodes.description: Day-two operational burden: upgrades, rebalancing, on-call load, and how much of the team's Kafka knowledge transfers.
nodes.output:
Redpanda removes ZooKeeper/KRaft operational surface and is genuinely simpler to run.

But: the team's accumulated Kafka knowledge is mostly about *consumers*, and that transfers unchanged (wire-compatible). The operational win is real but smaller than vendor material implies — it lands on the 2 engineers who already handle brokers, roughly 3 hrs/week each.

Verdict: mild pro-migration. Would flip if we were adding a third broker operator.

nodes.name: Lens: performance
nodes.description: Tests the premise itself — whether the current cluster genuinely cannot reach the Q3 target, rather than accepting that framing.
nodes.output:
The premise does not hold.

Replayed a peak-hour capture against the staging cluster: 240k msg/s sustained at 31% broker CPU. Extrapolating conservatively, the current 3-broker setup reaches ~700k msg/s before CPU saturation. The Q3 forecast fits inside existing hardware.

The p99 latency complaints that started this conversation trace to consumer-side batching in two services, not to broker throughput.

Verdict: strongly anti-migration. The stated problem is not a broker problem.

nodes.name: Lens: cost
nodes.description: Total cost of ownership counting the migration itself as a cost, not only the steady state after it.
nodes.output:
Steady state: Redpanda ~18% cheaper at this volume, roughly $1.4k/mo saved.

Migration: 2 engineers × ~7 weeks, dual-running both clusters for 3 of those weeks. Call it $95k fully loaded plus $4.2k of duplicate infrastructure.

Payback: ~5.6 years at current volume. Shortens to ~2 years only if volume triples and stays there.

Verdict: anti-migration on this volume.

nodes.name: Lens: risk
nodes.description: Cutover blast radius: what breaks, who notices, and how reversible each step is.
nodes.output:
Wire compatibility makes consumer cutover genuinely low-risk and reversible per consumer group.

The unreversible part is retained history: 14 days of retention would have to be either replayed or abandoned, and 3 of the 14 consumer groups do historical replay as part of normal recovery. Those 3 are the risk.

Verdict: neutral. Manageable, but it concentrates on the 3 groups we least want to disturb.

nodes.name: Fetch benchmarks
nodes.description: Cheap retrieval pass — pulls published benchmark numbers and hardware profiles for the performance lens to reason over.
nodes.output:
6 sources retrieved, 2 discarded as vendor-authored without methodology.
Usable: OpenMessaging 2024 run, two independent blog reproductions, one conference talk with raw data.

nodes.name: Scan incident history
nodes.description: Reads 18 months of internal incident reports for anything broker-attributed, so the ops lens argues from this cluster's actual history.
nodes.output:
41 incidents in 18 months. 4 touched Kafka:
  2 consumer lag from a downstream stall (not broker)
  1 disk pressure after a retention misconfiguration (operator error)
  1 genuine broker failure, recovered automatically in 90s

Broker-attributed downtime over 18 months: 90 seconds.

nodes.name: Synthesize
nodes.description: Reconciles four lenses that do not agree, and preserves the disagreement rather than averaging it away.
nodes.output:
Three of four lenses land anti-migration, and the fourth is only mildly pro.

The decisive finding is the performance lens overturning the premise: the question assumed a capacity ceiling that measurement does not support. Cost and risk then have nothing to buy.

Disagreement worth preserving: the ops lens's simplification argument stands on its own merits and will still be true later. This is a 'not now', not a 'never'.

nodes.name: Judge: evidence
nodes.description: Scores whether each claim is actually supported, with the benchmark replay held to the highest bar since the whole recommendation turns on it.
nodes.output:
Score 8/10. The replay is the strongest evidence in the set — real capture, real hardware, stated method.

Deduction: extrapolation from 31% CPU to saturation assumes linearity that was not tested above 240k. The headroom claim is directionally safe but numerically soft.

nodes.name: Judge: steelman
nodes.description: Adversarial pass — argues the migration case as strongly as possible to see whether the synthesis survives contact with its best opposition.
nodes.output:
Score 7/10. Best pro-migration case: this defers a migration that gets harder as consumer count grows, and 14 groups is already awkward.

But that argument does not beat a 5.6-year payback. The synthesis survives. Its 'not now, not never' framing is the right shape and I could not break it.

nodes.name: Judge: decision quality
nodes.description: Ignores the content and scores the decision itself — is it actionable, reversible, and does it name what would change the answer.
nodes.output:
Score 9/10. Actionable, cheap to revisit, and it names its own falsifier (sustained volume above ~500k msg/s).

Deduction: it should name a review date rather than leaving the revisit implicit.

nodes.name: Tally panel
nodes.description: Averages the three scores and folds each judge's deduction into the final wording.
nodes.output:
8.0 / 10 — accepted, with two amendments carried forward:
  · soften the headroom claim to the measured range
  · attach an explicit review trigger

nodes.name: Recommendation
nodes.description: Stay on Kafka through Q3. Fix consumer-side batching instead, and revisit if sustained volume passes 500k msg/s.
nodes.output:
ADR-0031 — Stay on Kafka through Q3

Measured headroom to ~700k msg/s on existing hardware (extrapolated from a 240k replay at 31% CPU; linearity untested above that point). The latency complaints that prompted this are consumer-side batching in checkout-ingest and audit-sink.

Actions:
  1. Fix batching in the two named services (owner: platform, this sprint)
  2. Re-run the replay at 400k to firm up the headroom number

Review trigger: sustained peak above 500k msg/s, or a third broker operator joining the team.

Run totals: 12 model calls, 153.7k tokens in, 23.6k out, $1.890, 6m 54s.

handoff.summary: Question plus current cluster shape and forecast

Filtered benchmark set with methodology notes
Grep 18 months of incidents for broker attribution
